spec.sequence: Coming along the track from the west, the line of boards shows first across the water, then the long house on the spit at their head and the stage shelter on the islet at their foot.
spec.wayfinding: The track meets the boards at their midpoint. The toll and the long house lie north; the islet and the ferry lie south, then east.

spec.value: The northern trunk's mid-point: a village strung along a channel because the channel is the street.
It lives on the ferry, the toll and feeding boat crews.
Alten Corimont's captain and Thorn's field-owners both think the toll should be theirs.
A day's run from either end of the trunk boat lane, which passes close enough to hail.
Would be bypassed if a deeper channel opened south.

value.loreSource: settlement-register row Riverwalk (M3 boardwalk village on the northern trunk); record occupants D1 households, D2 crews, D2 toll hands; notable slots toll-holder, stage-mistress
value.why: One household and the crews who stop the night share the long house. The spit is the only dry shelf big enough for a house; the islet takes a tent. Three plank walks join them, with a shrine and a ferry raft.

spec.cultureRole: a boardwalk household that keeps the long house
a boat crew stopping the night

spec.orientationWhy: Its door turns south-west to the head of the boards.

playerPurpose.note: Bunks let to boat crews stopping the night.
The household sells rope, food and boat stores.

compiledObjects.frontWhy: the band at 246° in the piece's own frame carries 1.35x the triangle density of a median band — the detailed face, which is the show side

spec.orientationWhy: Three spans run from the islet's north-east shore out to where the bed drops away.
The raft lies off the end of the landing for boarding.

compiledObjects.frontWhy: the source authors placed this piece 47 times with other statics to one side; the side they left open, at 11° in its own frame, is the front — and on an enclosure edge that open side is the outside

spec.orientationWhy: The spans turn east at the foot of the long walk and come ashore on the islet.
The totems face the long house yard.
Its open front turns west to the path from the islet walk.

sockets.why: The stores that the household sells to the crews, kept by the door.

sockets.why: The toll-holder keeps the takings in a painted urn by the long house door.
A stretch of boards laid at different times, the new planks paler than the old.
The household sleeps in the long house.
The household keeps the bunks and the stores in the long house.
The crew takes a bunk in the long house.
The crew poles the canoe and the raft along the lane.
The toll hand sleeps in the long house.
The toll hand keeps the shrine by the long house.
The stage-mistress sleeps in the long house.
The stage-mistress takes the fares under the stage shelter.
The toll-holder sleeps in the long house.
The toll-holder calls the toll from the long house door, at the head of the boards.
The toll-holder's tally of who paid which city.
The long house door, the most-used door in the village.
A household of the boards lets bunks to the crews and sells them stores.
A boat crew stopping the night, who poles the canoe for passengers.
A toll hand who backs the toll-holder in the nightly argument.
The stage-mistress runs the ferry from the shelter by the landing.
The toll-holder takes the toll from every boat and walker; the takings stay with the toll-holder.
The head of the ferry landing, where the stage-mistress takes the fares.
The head of the boards, where the toll-holder stops every walker.
Halfway along the boards, where the tracks from the west come onto them.
